If \(z_1, z_2 \in \mathbb{C}\) where \(z_1 = -3 + i\) and \(z_2 = 6 + 2i\), then the product

\[z_1 z_2 = \boxed{\phantom{-16 - 4i}}\]

Page 4

“Simple” Systems

Uncoupled systems are systems where each equation involves only one variable.

For an uncoupled system \(\dot{x} = ax\), \(\dot{y} = ay\), the solutions are:

\[x(t) = Ce^{at}, \quad y(t) = Ce^{at}\]

For a general uncoupled system \(\dot{x} = ax\), \(\dot{y} = by\) (with possibly different constants), the solutions decouple independently.

The question then becomes: what happens when we have \(\dot{x} = ax + by\)?

Page 5

Simple IVP 3 — Complex Uncoupled System

Solve for the solution curve \(\vec{r}(t) = \begin{pmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{pmatrix}\) so that \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\) and

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = x - 2y \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 2x + y \end{cases}\]

or equivalently

\[\vec{r}'(t) = \begin{pmatrix} x - 2y \\ 2x + y \end{pmatrix}.\]

Page 6

Simple IVP 3 — Solution (Step 1)

Let \(u = x + iy\). We group together the \(x\) and \(y\) parts:

\[\dot{u} = \dot{x} + i\dot{y} = (x - 2y) + i(2x + y)\]

Rearranging by collecting real and imaginary parts:

\[= (1 + 2i)x + (2 + (-1 \cdot i \cdot 2))\]

This simplifies to:

\[(2i + 1)(x + iy) = (1 + 2i)u\]

So the complex variable \(u = x + iy\) satisfies the simple scalar ODE:

\[\dot{u} = (1 + 2i)u\]

Page 7

Simple IVP 3 — Solution (Step 2)

Since \(\dot{u} = (1+2i)u\), this is now an uncoupled (simple) scalar ODE in \(u\).

The solution is:

\[u = Ce^{(1+2i)t}\]

Similarly, for \(v = x - iy\) (by replacing all \(i\) with \(-i\)):

\[\dot{v} = (1 - 2i)v\] \[v = De^{(1-2i)t}\]

Page 8

Simple IVP 3 — Solution (Step 3: Euler’s Formula)

Recall Euler’s formula: \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\)

Applying this to \(u\):

\[u = Ce^{(1+2i)t} = Ce^{t} e^{2it} = Ce^{t}(\cos(2t) + i\sin(2t))\]

Similarly for \(v\):

\[v = De^{(1-2i)t} = De^{t} e^{-2it} = De^{t}(\cos(2t) - i\sin(2t))\]

Page 9

Simple IVP 3 — Solution (Step 4: Substitute Back)

Recall \(u = x + iy\) and \(v = x - iy\), so:

\[x = \text{Re}(u) = \frac{u + v}{2}, \quad y = \text{Im}(u) = \frac{u - v}{2i}\]

Substituting the expressions for \(u\) and \(v\):

\[x = \text{Re}(u+v) = \text{Re}\!\left(Ce^{t}(\cos 2t + i\sin 2t) + De^{t}(\cos 2t - i\sin 2t)\right)\]

Page 10

Simple IVP 3 — Solution (Step 5: Collecting Terms)

Expanding \(u\):

\[u = Ce^{t}(\cos 2t + i\sin 2t)\]

Taking the real part and collecting terms (noting signs in the imaginary terms):

\[x(t) = \text{Re}(u) = e^{t}(C_1\cos 2t - C_1\sin 2t)\]

Taking the imaginary part:

\[y(t) = \text{Im}(u) = e^{t}(C_1\sin 2t + C_1\cos 2t)\]

where the constants \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) arise from absorbing \(C\) and \(D\).

Page 11

Simple IVP 3 — General Solution

General Solution:

From \(x = \text{Re}(u)\):

\[x(t) = e^{t}(C_1\cos 2t - C_2\sin 2t)\]

Similarly, by looking at \(y = \text{Im}(u)\):

\[y(t) = e^{t}(C_1\sin 2t + C_2\cos 2t)\]

These are the general solutions for the system.

Page 12

Simple IVP 3 — Applying Initial Conditions

Using the initial condition \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}\), i.e., \(x(0) = 1\) and \(y(0) = 1\):

\[x(0) = e^{0}(C_1\cos 0 - C_2\sin 0) = C_1 = 1\] \[y(0) = e^{0}(C_1\sin 0 + C_2\cos 0) = C_2 = 1\]

Therefore \(C_1 = 1\) and \(C_2 = 1\).

Particular Solution:

\[x(t) = e^{t}(\cos 2t - \sin 2t), \quad y(t) = e^{t}(\sin 2t + \cos 2t)\]

Page 13

Simple IVP 3 — Phase Portrait

Visual description: A GeoGebra phase portrait for the system \(x' = x - 2y\), \(y' = 2x + y\), displayed as a vector field of green arrows over the \(xy\)-plane. The arrows spiral outward from the origin counterclockwise, indicating an unstable spiral (source). A specific solution curve (red/pink spiral) starts at the initial condition \((1, 1)\) (shown as a blue dot) and spirals outward. Orange dots trace the numerical approximation along the curve. The display shows sliders \(C_1 = 1.1\) and \(C_2 = 1.1\) and the solution formulas: \(x(t) = e^t(\cos(2t) - \sin(2t))\) and \(y(t) = e^t(\sin(2t) + \cos(2t))\).

The spiral nature of the solution arises from the complex eigenvalue \(\lambda = 1 + 2i\): the real part \(a = 1 > 0\) causes exponential growth (outward spiral), and the imaginary part \(b = 2\) drives the rotation.

Page 14

Simple IVP 3 — General Observations

In General: For a system with complex eigenvalue \(a + bi\), the solutions take the form

\[e^{at}\begin{pmatrix}\cos(bt) - \sin(bt) \\ \sin(bt) + \cos(bt)\end{pmatrix}\]

(with constants \(C_1\), \(C_2\) absorbing initial conditions).

Observe:

  • \(a\) controls whether the spiral is a source (\(a > 0\), spiraling out) or a sink (\(a < 0\), spiraling in), and also controls the tightness of the spiral.
  • \(b\) controls the direction and speed of rotation of the spiral.

Simple IVP 3 — Activity

Solve for the solution curve \(\vec{r}(t) = \begin{pmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{pmatrix}\) so that \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}\) and

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -x + y \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = -y \end{cases}\]

or equivalently

\[\vec{r}'(t) = \begin{pmatrix} -x + y \\ -y \end{pmatrix}.\]

Page 16

Vectors

Definition: A vector in the plane is an ordered list of length 2 of numbers (real or complex). We visualize it as an arrow.

\[\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix}\]

Vectors can be given names (e.g., \(\mathbf{v}\), \(\mathbf{u}\)) and visualized as arrows in the plane pointing from the origin to the point \((a, b)\).

Page 17

Linear Combination

Definition: A linear combination of vectors \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) is a scaling and/or addition of the form:

\[c\mathbf{u} + d\mathbf{v}\]

where \(c, d\) are scalar constants.

A linear combination allows us to reach new vectors by stretching and adding existing ones.

Page 18

Linear Combination — Activity

(a) By moving points V and W, and sliders \(r\) and \(s\), in the GeoGebra applet below, create the mixture parallelogram for the linear combination \(-1\mathbf{v} + 1\mathbf{w}\).
